q: Butyraldehyde, CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO, has the systematic (IUPAC) name:
x: The –CHO group is always on C-1 of the chain, so the four-carbon aldehyde is simply butanal; no position number is needed. A ketone can never be on C-1.

q: Acetaldehyde is the common name of:
x: Acetaldehyde, CH₃CHO, is ethanal. Methanal is formaldehyde and propanone is acetone.

q: Methyl propyl ketone, CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₃, is named by IUPAC rules as:
x: The chain has five carbons and the C=O is given the lowest number, C-2, so it is pentan-2-one. 'Pentan-4-one' numbers from the wrong end.

q: The smallest possible ketone contains how many carbon atoms?
x: In a ketone the carbonyl carbon must be bonded to two other carbon atoms, so the smallest is propanone, CH₃COCH₃, with three carbons. One- and two-carbon carbonyl compounds are aldehydes.

q: The arrangement of the three atoms bonded to the carbonyl carbon of propanone is:
o: Trigonal planar, with bond angles of about 120°
Tetrahedral, with bond angles of about 109.5°
Linear, with a bond angle of 180°
Pyramidal, with bond angles of about 107°
x: The carbonyl carbon is sp² hybridised, so its three σ bonds lie in one plane at about 120°. The π bond lies above and below that plane.

q: The carbon–oxygen double bond of a carbonyl group consists of:
o: One σ bond and two π bonds
One σ bond and one π bond
x: Every double bond has one σ bond (head-on overlap of sp² and p orbitals) and one π bond (sideways overlap of unhybridised p orbitals).

q: Aldehydes and ketones boil higher than alkanes, but lower than alcohols, of similar molar mass. This is because their molecules:
o: Have dipole–dipole attractions but cannot hydrogen-bond to each other
Hydrogen-bond to each other more strongly than alcohols do
Are ionic in the liquid state
x: The polar C=O group gives dipole–dipole forces, stronger than the dispersion forces of alkanes. They have no H on oxygen, so they cannot hydrogen-bond among themselves as alcohols do.

q: Which is the correct IUPAC name for the ketone (CH₃)₂CHCOCH₃?
x: The main chain has four carbons; numbering from the end nearer the C=O puts it on C-2 and the methyl on C-3. '2-Methylbutan-3-one' gives the carbonyl a higher number; 3-methylbutanal and pentan-2-one are isomers.

q: Vapour of propan-2-ol is passed over heated copper at about 300 °C. The organic product is:
x: Hot copper removes hydrogen (dehydrogenation): (CH₃)₂CHOH → CH₃COCH₃ + H₂. A secondary alcohol gives a ketone; propanal would come from propan-1-ol.

q: Ethyne is passed into dilute sulphuric acid containing mercury(II) sulphate at about 80 °C. The product is:
x: Water adds across the triple bond to give an unstable enol, CH₂=CHOH, which rearranges to ethanal, CH₃CHO. The Hg²⁺ ion catalyses the hydration.

q: Propyne, CH₃C≡CH, is hydrated using dilute H₂SO₄ and HgSO₄. The main product is:
x: By Markovnikov's rule the –OH of the enol goes to the middle carbon, CH₃C(OH)=CH₂, which rearranges to the ketone CH₃COCH₃. Only ethyne gives an aldehyde by this method.

q: 2-Methylpropene, (CH₃)₂C=CH₂, is treated with ozone and the ozonide is then warmed with zinc dust and water. The products are:
x: The C=C bond is cut and each carbon becomes C=O: (CH₃)₂C= gives (CH₃)₂C=O (propanone) and =CH₂ gives HCHO (methanal).

q: Benzene reacts with ethanoyl chloride (CH₃COCl) in the presence of anhydrous AlCl₃. The product is:
x: This is Friedel–Crafts acylation: the CH₃CO⁺ electrophile substitutes into the ring, giving the aromatic ketone phenylethanone (acetophenone) and HCl. Ethylbenzene would need an alkyl halide.

q: Mild, controlled oxidation of methanol gives:
x: A primary alcohol is oxidised first to an aldehyde, so CH₃OH gives HCHO (methanal). Further oxidation would give methanoic acid.

q: On controlled oxidation with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, which pair of alcohols gives an aldehyde and a ketone respectively?
x: Primary propan-1-ol gives propanal (aldehyde); secondary propan-2-ol gives propanone (ketone). Tertiary 2-methylpropan-2-ol is not oxidised, and methanol gives an aldehyde.

q: 6.0 g of propan-1-ol (M = 60) is oxidised and 4.35 g of propanal (M = 58) is collected. What is the percentage yield? (1 mol alcohol gives 1 mol aldehyde)
x: 0.1 mol propan-1-ol gives at most 0.1 mol × 58 = 5.8 g propanal. Yield = 4.35/5.8 × 100 = 75%. 72.5% wrongly compares 4.35 g with the 6.0 g of alcohol.

q: Benzaldehyde, C₆H₅CHO, is less reactive than ethanal towards nucleophilic addition. The main reason is that:
o: The benzene ring makes the carbonyl carbon more positive
The benzene ring donates electron density to the carbonyl carbon by resonance, reducing its positive charge
Benzaldehyde has no hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon
Benzaldehyde has an sp³ carbonyl carbon
x: Conjugation of the C=O with the ring spreads π electron density onto the carbonyl carbon, lowering its δ+ charge, so nucleophiles attack it less readily. Benzaldehyde does have an H on its carbonyl carbon.

q: In the carbonyl group of an aldehyde, the partial charges are:
x: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so it pulls the bonding electrons towards itself and becomes δ−, leaving the carbon δ+.

q: Aldehydes behave as reducing agents because they:
o: Are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids
x: A reducing agent is itself oxidised. The H on the aldehyde carbonyl carbon lets aldehydes be oxidised readily to acids, so they reduce Ag⁺ and Cu²⁺.

q: A ketone carrying two very bulky alkyl groups, such as (CH₃)₃CCOC(CH₃)₃, adds nucleophiles extremely slowly. This is mainly because:
o: The carbonyl carbon carries a large positive charge
The C=O bond in it is non-polar
The bulky groups hinder the approach of the nucleophile to the carbonyl carbon
x: Large groups crowd the carbonyl carbon (steric hindrance) and also release electrons, so a nucleophile approaches with difficulty. This is the same effect, in a stronger form, that makes ketones less reactive than aldehydes.

q: In reactions of the carbonyl group, an electrophile such as H⁺ attaches to:
o: A hydrogen atom of the alkyl group
x: The oxygen is δ− and carries lone pairs, so electrophiles such as H⁺ bond to it. Nucleophiles attack the δ+ carbonyl carbon.

q: Trichloroethanal (chloral), CCl₃CHO, is more reactive than ethanal towards nucleophiles. This is because the –CCl₃ group:
o: Releases electrons and decreases the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon
Withdraws electrons and increases the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon
Makes the carbonyl carbon sp³ hybridised
Removes the hydrogen from the carbonyl carbon
x: The three electronegative chlorine atoms pull electrons away, making the carbonyl carbon more δ+ and so more attractive to nucleophiles. Electron-releasing alkyl groups have the opposite effect.

q: Which statement correctly compares the reactions of aldehydes and ketones?
o: On reduction, aldehydes give secondary alcohols and ketones give primary alcohols
On reduction, aldehydes give primary alcohols and ketones give secondary alcohols
x: Adding H₂ across C=O turns RCHO into RCH₂OH (primary) and RCOR′ into RCH(OH)R′ (secondary). Both classes give 2,4-DNPH precipitates and both undergo nucleophilic addition.

q: Methanal, HCHO, differs from all other aldehydes because its carbonyl carbon is bonded to:
o: One hydrogen atom and one alkyl group
One alkyl group and one –OH group
x: In methanal both remaining bonds of the carbonyl carbon go to H atoms. Other aldehydes have one H and one alkyl or aryl group; ketones have two carbon groups.

q: In the base-catalysed addition of HCN to a carbonyl compound, the step that forms the new C–C bond is:
o: Attack of H⁺ on the carbonyl oxygen
Attack of CN⁻ on the carbonyl oxygen
Attack of CN⁻ on the carbonyl carbon, giving an alkoxide ion
Attack of HCN molecules on the α-carbon
x: The cyanide ion, a nucleophile, attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon and the π electrons move onto oxygen, forming an alkoxide ion. This then takes H⁺ from HCN, giving the cyanohydrin.

q: The cyanohydrin obtained from acetone (propanone) has the formula:
x: H adds to the oxygen and CN to the carbonyl carbon: (CH₃)₂C=O + HCN → (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN, 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile. CH₃CH(OH)CN is the cyanohydrin of ethanal.

q: Propanone reacts with hydroxylamine, NH₂OH, in weakly acidic solution. The organic product is:
x: NH₂OH adds to the C=O and then water is lost (addition–elimination), giving propanone oxime, (CH₃)₂C=NOH. Hydrazine, not hydroxylamine, gives a hydrazone.

q: In acid-catalysed nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl compound, H⁺ speeds up the reaction because protonating the oxygen:
o: Turns the nucleophile into a stronger base
Removes the α-hydrogen from the molecule
Makes the carbonyl carbon more positive and so more easily attacked by weak nucleophiles
x: When the oxygen is protonated, the positive charge is shared with the carbonyl carbon, which becomes much more electrophilic. Even weak nucleophiles such as water, alcohols or NH₂OH can then add.

q: Which compound does NOT undergo aldol condensation with dilute alkali?
x: Aldol condensation needs a hydrogen on the α-carbon (next to C=O), which the base removes to make a carbanion. Methanal, HCHO, has no α-carbon at all; the other three have α-hydrogens.

q: The Cannizzaro reaction, in which an aldehyde is warmed with concentrated NaOH to give an alcohol and a carboxylate salt, is shown by aldehydes that:
o: Have at least two α-hydrogen atoms
Are ketones with a methyl group
x: Aldehydes without α-hydrogen, such as methanal and benzaldehyde, cannot form a carbanion and so cannot do aldol condensation; instead one molecule is oxidised and another reduced (Cannizzaro).

q: Two molecules of propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO, combine in dilute NaOH. The aldol product is:
x: The base removes an α-H from CH₂, and the carbanion CH₃CH⁻CHO attacks the C=O of a second molecule, giving CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH(CH₃)CHO: 3-hydroxy-2-methylpentanal. 3-Hydroxybutanal is the aldol from ethanal.

q: Butanal, CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO, is reduced with NaBH₄. The product is:
x: Reduction of an aldehyde adds two H atoms across the C=O, giving a primary alcohol, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH (butan-1-ol). Butan-2-ol would come from the ketone butanone.

q: Cyclohexanone, C₆H₁₀O, is reduced with sodium borohydride. The product is:
x: NaBH₄ reduces the ketone C=O to CH–OH, giving the secondary alcohol cyclohexanol. It does not remove the oxygen to give cyclohexane, and it does not open the ring.

q: Reducing the aromatic aldehyde C₆H₅CHO with lithium aluminium hydride gives:
x: The –CHO group becomes –CH₂OH, so the product is benzyl alcohol (phenylmethanol). Benzoic acid would be the oxidation product, not the reduction product.

q: Which reagent would NOT convert butanone into butan-2-ol?
o: LiAlH₄ in dry ether, then dilute acid
x: Butanone → butan-2-ol is a reduction. NaBH₄, LiAlH₄ and H₂/Ni are reducing agents; acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ is an oxidising agent, so it cannot do this.

q: 2.9 g of propanone (M = 58) is completely reduced to propan-2-ol (M = 60). What mass of propan-2-ol is formed?
x: Moles of propanone = 2.9/58 = 0.05 mol, giving 0.05 mol of propan-2-ol = 0.05 × 60 = 3.0 g. The mass rises slightly because two H atoms are added.

q: A carbonyl compound X, C₅H₁₀O, is reduced by NaBH₄ to pentan-3-ol, CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CH₃. X is:
x: Reduction turns C=O into CH–OH at the same position, so the –OH on C-3 must come from a C=O on C-3: CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃, pentan-3-one. Pentanal would give pentan-1-ol.

q: When propanal is reduced to propan-1-ol, how many hydrogen atoms are added to each molecule?
x: CH₃CH₂CHO (C₃H₆O) becomes CH₃CH₂CH₂OH (C₃H₈O): one H goes to the carbonyl carbon and one to the oxygen, two H atoms in all.

q: Ethanal is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate. The organic product is:
x: Aldehydes are easily oxidised: CH₃CHO + [O] → CH₃COOH. Ethanol would be the reduction product.

q: Which reagent gives a brick-red precipitate with ethanal but no change with propanone?
x: Ethanal reduces the Cu²⁺ of Fehling's solution to red Cu₂O; propanone is not oxidised. Both compounds react with 2,4-DNPH, with sodium hydrogensulphite and with iodine in alkali, so those cannot tell them apart.

q: In the silver mirror test, how many moles of Ag⁺ are reduced to silver for each mole of propanal oxidised?
x: The aldehyde is oxidised to a carboxylate, losing two electrons per molecule; each Ag⁺ gains one electron, so 2 mol Ag⁺ are reduced: RCHO + 2Ag⁺ → ... + 2Ag.

q: The only aldehyde that gives a positive iodoform (triiodomethane) test is:
x: The iodoform test needs a CH₃CO– group. Among aldehydes only ethanal, CH₃CHO, has a methyl group joined to the carbonyl carbon.

q: When an aldehyde is warmed with Fehling's solution, a positive result is a colour change from:
o: Deep blue to a brick-red precipitate
x: Fehling's solution is deep blue because of Cu²⁺; the aldehyde reduces this to Cu₂O, a brick-red precipitate. Orange to green is the change for acidified dichromate.

q: X, C₄H₈O, gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent. On oxidation it gives 2-methylpropanoic acid, (CH₃)₂CHCOOH. X is:
x: The silver mirror shows X is an aldehyde, and oxidation keeps the carbon skeleton, so X is (CH₃)₂CHCHO. Butanal would give butanoic acid; butanone is a ketone and 2-methylpropan-1-ol is C₄H₁₀O.

q: Which compound is NOT oxidised by Tollens' reagent?
x: Tollens' reagent is a mild oxidising agent that oxidises aldehydes, including aromatic benzaldehyde, but not ketones. Butanone, a ketone, gives no silver mirror.
